questions.topic: Modal interchange and the chords it borrows
questions.learningObjective: State what modal interchange borrows

stimulus.body: Read this source excerpt carefully: «The iv chord from the parallel minor.» Modal interchange can borrow the iv chord from the parallel minor. A marginal reminder adds: think parallel minor borrowing. It is followed by four candidate interpretations, of which exactly one is supported by the wording of the excerpt.

questions.stem: The prompt gives “State what modal interchange borrows / Think parallel minor borrowing. / Modal interchange and the chords it borrows” as the nudge. Which option is really supported?

options.text: The vii chord from the relative minor
The I chord from the same key
options.misconception: treats "The I chord from the same key" as if it followed from the evidence

options.text: The V chord from the dominant key
The iv chord from the parallel minor

questions.explanation: Close reading of the note yields this rule: modal interchange can borrow the iv chord from the parallel minor. On that basis "The iv chord from the parallel minor" is the supported choice. Option A ("The vii chord from the relative minor") fails because it confuses with relative modulation; Option B ("The I chord from the same key") fails because it treats "The I chord from the same key" as if it followed from the evidence; Option C ("The V chord from the dominant key") fails because it confuses with secondary dominant.

questions.stem: Before selecting, apply “Count notes a borrowed chord adds / Compare borrowed chord tones to the key. / How many notes a borrowed chord adds” to the passage. Which answer holds up?

options.text: Three notes, adding the flattened seventh
Two notes, the flattened third and sixth

options.misconception: mistakes a surface feature of "Zero notes, staying diatonic" for the governing rule

questions.explanation: What settles the item is the relation stated in the passage: a borrowed bVI introduces one note outside the key, the flattened sixth. On that basis "One note, the flattened sixth" is the supported choice. Option A ("Three notes, adding the flattened seventh") fails because it overcounts further; Option B ("Two notes, the flattened third and sixth") fails because it overcounts altered notes; Option D ("Zero notes, staying diatonic") fails because it mistakes a surface feature of "Zero notes, staying diatonic" for the governing rule.
